fatigue.instrument: Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire (CFQ), Likert scoring 0,1,2,3; range 0-33; higher = more fatigue
fatigue.evidence_quote: At 12 weeks, compared with the control group, mean fatigue score was 19·1 (SD 7·6) in the GES group and 22·9 (6·9) in the control group (adjusted difference −4·2 points, 95% CI −6·1 to −2·3, p<0·0001; effect size 0·53).

harms.definition: Serious adverse events (1% GES vs 2% control); 0 serious adverse reactions in either arm; also reported: worsened CGI-health 1 (1%) GES vs 8 (8%) control (p=0.04, Fisher's exact); worsened CGI-CFS 0 GES vs 9 (9%) control (p=0.003); composite serious-deterioration criterion (SF-36 PF drop ≥10, CGI 'much/very much worse', or active withdrawal due to worsening) 20 (21%) GES vs 30 (30%) control, p=0.14.
harms.note: No serious adverse reactions to trial interventions in either group; safety signals favoured GES on worsening measures.

notes: GETSET is a two-arm pragmatic RCT: guided graded exercise SELF-HELP (GES; booklet + up to 4 brief physiotherapist guidance sessions, max 90 min total, no direct therapist-led exercise sessions) plus specialist medical care (SMC), vs SMC alone (no non-exercise psychological/pacing arm). This is a lower-intensity, self-help variant of GET (distinct from PACE's therapist-delivered GET) but is coded as GET-vs-control per the review's classification since it is graded-exercise-based. Two co-primary outcomes (added mid-trial per protocol amendment, approved by ethics/DMEC/TSC before outcome data examined): CFQ fatigue and SF-36 PF physical function, both at 12 weeks, modified ITT. Both outcomes are per-arm mean/SD plus adjusted between-group difference from Table 3 (identical to abstract numbers). Physical function: GES 55.7 (SD 23.3, n=97) vs control 50.8 (SD 25.3, n=102); adjusted MD +6.3 (95% CI 1.8 to 10.8), p=0.006, effect size 0.20 (higher=better). Diagnostic criteria: NICE (primary), with subgroup analyses also reported meeting Oxford and CDC (Fukuda) criteria. Age: adults (18+). RoB: open-label (patients and physiotherapists unmasked; statistician masked to allocation); both primary outcomes are self-rated (high risk of performance/detection bias, typical for GET trials); randomization was computer-generated block randomization stratified by centre, depression score, and baseline physical function — concealment mechanism not explicitly detailed in the excerpted text; attrition: 97/107 (91%) GES and 102/104 (98%) control had 12-week outcome data (safety table shows n=97 GES / n=101 control, slightly different denominator for safety analysis).

physical_function.evidence_quote: mean physical function score was 55·7 (23·3) in the GES group and 50·8 (25·3) in the control group (adjusted difference 6·3 points, 1·8 to 10·8, p=0·006; 0·20).

rob_notes: Open-label: "Patients and physiotherapists were necessarily unmasked from intervention assignment; the statistician was masked from intervention assignment." Randomization: block randomisation (randomly varying block sizes) at individual level, computer-generated sequence, stratified by centre, depression score, and severity of physical disability (allocation-concealment mechanism not detailed in text excerpted here). Both primary outcomes (CFQ fatigue, SF-36 PF) are self-rated by patients -> high risk of performance and detection bias given lack of participant/therapist blinding, standard limitation for GET/self-help trials. Attrition: 97/107 (GES) and 102/104 (control) had 12-week primary outcome data (modified ITT, i.e., all randomised with follow-up data included regardless of adherence). Two co-primary outcomes were established mid-recruitment (protocol amendment after 47% enrolled, before outcome data seen, approved by ethics/DMEC/TSC) — reduces (but does not eliminate) outcome-switching concern. No blinding of outcome assessment beyond the statistician.

usable_reason: Genuine two-arm GET(-self-help)-vs-non-exercise-control (SMC alone) trial with complete per-arm n/mean/SD at the designated primary end-of-treatment timepoint (12 weeks) for both fatigue (CFQ) and physical function (SF-36 PF), plus adjusted between-group MD and 95% CI/p for each — fully usable for SMD/MD pooling.

harms.definition: Serious adverse events (death, hospital admission, increased severe and persistent disability, self-harm, life-threatening, or intervention required to prevent one of these); GET also had serious adverse reactions and a 'serious deterioration' composite (SF-36 PF drop ≥20 at two consecutive visits, PCGI much/very much worse at two consecutive visits, withdrawal due to explicit worsening, or serious adverse reaction)
harms.note: Participants with serious adverse events: GET 13 (8%) of 160 vs SMC 7 (4%) of 160 (event counts 17 vs 7). Serious adverse reactions: GET 2 (1%) vs SMC 2 (1%). Serious deterioration composite: GET 10 (6%) vs SMC 15 (9%), difference vs SMC = -3.1%, p=0.30. No suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions in any group. [harms metric = participants with >=1 SAE: GET 13/160 vs SMC 7/160]

notes: 4-arm trial (APT, CBT, GET, SMC alone), n=641 randomized. Primary GET-vs-control contrast used here is GET vs SMC alone (the non-exercise, non-CBT/APT usual-care control), matching the paper's own primary reported comparison table (Table 3, 'Mean difference (95% CI) from SMC (52 weeks)'). GET vs APT is also reported in the same table if a secondary pairwise contrast is wanted: fatigue MD -2.5 (-4.2 to -0.9), p=0.0059; physical function MD 12.8 (7.7 to 17.9), p<0.0001. Values converted from the source's middle-dot decimal notation (e.g. '20·6' -> 20.6). Bonferroni-adjusted p for GET vs SMC: fatigue p=0.0013, physical function p=0.0025 (adjusted for 5 comparisons per outcome); unadjusted values reported above per the 'between_group' fields to match the schema's single p slot, with adjusted=false. Diagnostic criteria = Oxford (explicitly stated); adults recruited from six UK secondary-care clinics. Blinding: participants, therapists, doctors, and research assessors were NOT masked (open-label); primary outcomes were self-rated by participants; only the analysis statistician was masked to allocation — classic high risk of performance/detection bias for a GET trial with subjective self-report primary outcomes. Randomization: computer-generated sequence via independent Clinical Trials Unit database programmer, first 3 participants per centre simple randomization then centre-stratified minimisation — allocation concealment appears adequate (central allocation, independent of trial team).

rob_notes: Randomization: computer-generated sequence, centrally administered by an independent database programmer at the Clinical Trials Unit, stratified by centre with probabilistic minimisation (first 3 participants/centre simple randomization) — low risk, adequate allocation concealment. Blinding: open-label — participants, therapists, and treating doctors could not be masked (nature of intervention); research assessors were also unmasked (deemed impractical); ONLY the statistician analyzing primary outcomes was masked to allocation. Primary outcomes (Chalder fatigue, SF-36 PF) are entirely self-rated by participants — high risk of performance and detection bias typical of open-label GET trials with subjective primary endpoints. Attrition: primary outcome data available for large majority (n=148-154 of 159-161 per arm at 52 weeks, ~93-96% retention), analysis included all participants with available primary-outcome data (not strict ITT for 100% of randomized). Independent, masked adverse-event scrutinisers used for harms adjudication (unmasked only afterward to classify serious adverse reactions) — good practice for the safety outcomes specifically.

harms.note: No serious adverse events or dropout-due-to-harm counts reported by arm. Only completion/attendance is reported: 6-month follow-up completed measures BUC 54/75 (72%), GET 51/71 (71.8%), COUNS 58/76 (76.3%); 12-month: BUC 57/75 (76%), GET 53/71 (73.2%), COUNS 64/76 (85.5%). Full treatment (attended all 8 sessions): BUC 75/75 (100%, received usual care by definition), GET 38/71 (53.5%), COUNS 42/76 (55.3%).

notes: Three-arm trial (BUC usual-care-plus-CBT-booklet vs GET vs Counselling) in UK primary care, patients referred by GPs for fatigue >3 months (not a specialist CFS/ME cohort defined by Oxford/Fukuda/CCC criteria - eligibility was pragmatic: age 16-75, fatigue as main problem >=3 months, normal FBC/ESR/TFT, fatigue scale score >=4, excluding physical/psychiatric causes). Randomized 1:1:1, block randomization (size 9) by a separate-site statistician using sequential sealed opaque envelopes - reasonable allocation concealment. Open-label (no blinding of participants/therapists possible for GET vs usual care); outcome (Chalder fatigue) is self-reported questionnaire mailed home - high risk of performance and detection bias typical of GET trials. Attrition: 6-month follow-up only 163/222 (73%) overall, fairly balanced across arms; ITT approach with multiple imputation used, complete-case results also reported (Table 3 uses complete-case observed means, since NEJM-style regression estimates reported separately in text with similar effect sizes). No physical-function outcome (no SF-36 PF subscale, no 6-minute walk test) was measured/reported in this trial - only fatigue (Chalder), HADS anxiety/depression, WSAS (work/social adjustment, a functional-impairment measure but not a physical-function scale), and patient satisfaction. Therefore physical_function fields are left null/not_reported. Both per-arm means/SDs (Table 3, observed/complete-case) and adjusted between-group mean differences with 95% CI/p (from mixed linear regression, unadjusted per authors since RCT) are available and are consistent with each other. 12-month (longer-term) fatigue result: GET -0.06 (95% CI -1.8 to 1.6) vs BUC, p=0.94 - included in trial narrative but NOT used as primary timepoint per instructions (using 6-month primary endpoint instead).
rob_notes: Randomization: computer/statistician-generated block randomization (blocks of size 9) performed at a separate site - low risk. Allocation concealment: sequential numbered opaque sealed envelopes opened in front of patient at baseline by research assistant - adequate concealment at allocation, though envelope methods carry some residual risk if not tamper-evident. Blinding: open-label design; participants and therapists necessarily unblinded to GET vs usual care vs counselling assignment - high risk of performance bias. Primary outcome (Chalder fatigue score) is self-reported questionnaire completed at home and mailed in - high risk of detection/reporting bias given lack of blinding. Attrition: substantial loss to follow-up at 6 months (163/222, ~73% retained) and 12 months (174/222, ~78%), but missingness not significantly associated with allocated group (p=0.78 at 6mo, p=0.36 at 12mo); handled via ITT with multiple imputation (MAR assumption) alongside complete-case analysis - moderate risk given differential completion of \"full treatment\" (100% BUC vs ~54% GET/COUNS attended all 8 sessions, though this reflects treatment adherence not outcome-assessment attrition). Overall: typical open-label GET-trial risk-of-bias profile - high risk of performance/detection bias, otherwise reasonably conducted randomization/allocation.

usable_reason: Genuine three-arm RCT with a GET arm vs a non-exercise usual-care control (BUC) plus a counselling arm; per-arm means/SDs and between-group mean difference with 95% CI/p at the primary 6-month end-of-treatment timepoint are reported for the Chalder Fatigue Scale, making it usable for the primary fatigue pool. No physical-function outcome was measured in this trial, so it cannot contribute to a physical-function pooled analysis.

harms.definition: Adverse events (not further defined); dropouts reported separately (not attributed to harm)
harms.note: Text states: 'both treatment interventions were well tolerated by the individuals with no adverse events being recorded.' Separately, withdrawals: RT arm n=2 (1 due to injury restricting ability to complete intervention, 1 wanted to complete both interventions instead); AT arm n=1 (didn't want to complete programme). Handled via last-observation-carried-forward for ITT, not exclusion.

rob_notes: Randomization via envelope-draw of 40 slips (20 RT/20 AT) with the drawn slip replaced into the envelope before resealing -- weak/unclear allocation concealment and risk of imbalance. Single-blind design: only the outcome assessor was blinded; participants and the treating exercise physiologist were not blinded (open-label active-comparator trial), and outcomes are self-report questionnaires (SF-36, FSS, BDI) = high risk of performance and detection bias. Explicitly a pilot trial with no power calculation, n=11/arm. One missing data point imputed via last-observation-carried-forward. No non-exercising standard-care control arm -- authors explicitly acknowledge this as a limitation.
usable_reason: Both arms are active exercise interventions (graded aerobic training vs progressive resistance training) with no non-exercise comparator (no usual-care/SMC, waitlist, CBT, pacing, or relaxation control). This is a head-to-head exercise-modality comparison, explicitly acknowledged by the authors as lacking a standard-care control group ('limited by ... the lack of a non-exercising, standard care control group'). Per task instructions this must be excluded from the primary GET-vs-control pool (is_get_vs_control=false, usable_for_primary_pool=false). Data are reported for completeness only; the 'AT' arm is mapped to get_arm and 'RT' arm to control_arm purely for schema compliance, not because RT functions as a true control.
notes: Trial: Gordon BA, Knapman LM, Lubitz L. "Graduated exercise training and progressive resistance training in adolescents with chronic fatigue syndrome: a randomized controlled pilot study." Clin Rehabil 2010;24:1072-1079. Single-blind pilot RCT, n=22 adolescents (13-18y, Fukuda-CDC criteria), 4-week inpatient programme, 5 days/week. GET arm = graded aerobic exercise training (stationary cycling + treadmill, 20-40 min); comparator = progressive resistance training (16 exercises, single set, moderate load/high reps) -- NOT a non-exercise control. No between-group difference on any outcome (fatigue, SF-36 PCS, exercise tolerance, strength, depression); both arms improved significantly from baseline on most measures. Authors explicitly flag lack of non-exercising standard-care control group as a key limitation. Because there is no GET-vs-non-exercise-control contrast, this trial should be excluded from the primary meta-analytic pool per protocol, though it could be cited narratively as evidence that GET and resistance training produce similar effects, or included in a sensitivity analysis of exercise-vs-exercise trials.

fatigue.evidence_quote: There was little evidence of differences between groups in the secondary outcome measures (Supplementary Table 2). The allocated groups saw similar improvements over time in mean Chalder Fatigue scores.

harms.definition: Serious adverse events requiring hospital treatment; withdrawal from allocated therapy due to feeling worse
harms.note: Four SAEs total requiring hospital treatment: one event in each of 2 AM participants, two events in 1 GET participant; one SAE (psychiatric hospital admission for suicidal ideation) possibly related to GET. Withdrew due to feeling worse: 4/117 (3%) GET, 1/123 (1%) AM (note paper's n-denominators appear swapped in text). Composite deterioration (from at least one measure: CGI, SF-36-PFS drop ≥20pts, clinician report, or withdrawal-due-to-worsening): 33/123 (27%) GET vs 20/117 (17%) AM, p=0.069.

notes: MAGENTA is a pragmatic, open-label, two-arm parallel RCT: GET vs Activity Management (AM, a non-exercise 'energy management'/pacing-style personalised approach managing cognitive, school and physical activity). This is a genuine GET-vs-non-exercise-control comparison; AM is coded as control_type 'other' because it's not exactly usual-care/waitlist/CBT/pacing-APT/relaxation but is closest to a pacing/activity-management comparator (similar in spirit to APT). Primary outcome and only outcome with full per-arm mean/SD reported in the main text is SF-36 physical function subscale (SF-36-PFS) at 6 months (Table 3). Chalder Fatigue scale was a SECONDARY outcome; the main-text/PDF only states qualitatively that 'the allocated groups saw similar improvements over time in mean Chalder Fatigue scores' — exact 6-month per-arm mean/SD/between-group values are in Supplementary Table 2, which was not available in the local PDF or converted body.md (only baseline Chalder means were found: GET 24.5 (SD 5.0) n=119; AM 24.0 (SD 4.9) n=115 — these are BASELINE, not the end-of-treatment outcome, so not used to populate the primary/EOT fields). Recommend sourcing the online supplementary material (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-024-05458-x supplementary Table 2) if precise 6-month Chalder numbers are needed for the pooled fatigue meta-analysis; until then this trial should be treated as usable for physical function (SF-36-PFS) but NOT usable for the fatigue pool (reported=not_reported, confidence=low). Diagnostic criteria: 2007 NICE criteria for ME/CFS (not Oxford/Fukuda/CCC/ICC). Age group: pediatric (8-17 years, mean ~14.3). RoB: open-label/unblinded (participants, parents, clinicians all aware of allocation) — high risk of performance bias; self-reported primary outcome (SF-36-PFS) = high risk of detection/reporting bias for a subjective measure; randomization via web-based system with minimisation by age and sex (adequate allocation concealment plausible given central web-based randomization); ITT primary analysis with multiple imputation sensitivity analyses; attrition: 103/123 (84%) GET and 98/118 (83%) AM included in 6-month primary analysis, dropping further to 59% at 12 months in both arms (differential attrition risk to long-term but not 6-month primary timepoint).

physical_function.evidence_quote: 6-month scores 55.7 (23.3), 103 57.7 (26.0), 98 − 2.02 (− 7.75, 3.70) 0.49 [Table 3, SF-36-PF at 6 months (primary outcome)]; also in text: 'the mean SF-36-PFS score changed from 54.8 (standard deviation 23.7) to 55.7 (23.3) for GET and from 55.5 (23.1) to 57.7 (26.0) for AM giving an adjusted difference in means of −2.02 (95% confidence interval −7.75, 2.70)' [Abstract; note abstract CI upper bound '2.70' appears to be a typo for Table 3's '3.70']

rob_notes: Open-label RCT: "This study was necessarily unmasked, with participants, parents and clinicians, aware of allocation." Randomization: web-based system (Bristol Trials Centre) with minimisation by age (8-12 vs 13-17) and sex, weighted 0.8 — adequate allocation concealment via central web-based system. Primary outcome (SF-36-PFS) is self-reported = high risk of detection bias given lack of blinding (performance/detection bias typical of GET trials). ITT primary analysis (multivariable linear regression adjusting for baseline outcome, age, sex); sensitivity analyses for missing data (multiple imputation, MAR assumption) supported same conclusions. Attrition at 6-month primary timepoint: 103/123 (84%) GET, 98/118 (83%) AM analyzed — relatively low/balanced attrition at primary timepoint, but rises to ~59% completion in both arms by 12 months (secondary timepoint). Adherence/fidelity: mean of only 3.9 (GET) and 4.6 (AM) sessions attended by 6 months — very low treatment dose ("this lack of improvement...may be explained by the low intensity of therapy sessions" per Conclusions), which affects interpretation of a null effect (fidelity issue, not necessarily blinding-related bias). Registered prospectively (ISRCTN23962803, 3 Sept 2015) before enrolment; primary outcome was however only confirmed in the full trial protocol after the feasibility phase had already collected some data, raising some outcome-switching concern (acknowledged by authors in Discussion).

usable_reason: Genuine GET-vs-non-exercise-control (Activity Management) parallel RCT with full per-arm mean/SD/N for the primary outcome (SF-36-PFS) at the pre-specified 6-month primary end-of-treatment timepoint, plus the adjusted between-group mean difference and 95% CI — usable for the physical-function pool. NOT usable for the fatigue pool at present because exact 6-month per-arm Chalder Fatigue means/SDs are only in Supplementary Table 2, which was not locally available (only qualitative "similar improvements" text and BASELINE Chalder means could be sourced).

control_arm_label: Appointments only (exercise-control / non-exercise), pooled across fluoxetine and placebo-drug sub-arms

fatigue.timepoint: 26 weeks (6 months, trial's designated end-of-treatment assessment; also had week 12 interim)
fatigue.evidence_quote: There were trends for exercise to improve fatigue scale scores at week 12 (n=136, mean change=2.l (95% CI -0.6 to 4.8); F(1,132)=2.36, P=0.13) and at week 26 (n=136, mean change=2.9 (95% CI -0.2 to 6.1); F(1,132)=3.35, P=0.07).

get_arm_label: Graded exercise (with fluoxetine or placebo drug), pooled across drug factor

harms.note: No formal adverse-event/SAE table by arm reported. Paper reports overall drop-out rate higher with exercise than non-exercise (25/68 (37%) vs 15/69 (22%), Cox proportional hazards P=0.05) and that 11 subjects dropped out due to medication side-effects (2 taking placebo drug) - not broken down by exercise arm. No exercise-specific harm/injury counts given.

notes: This is a 2x2 FACTORIAL trial (exercise vs exercise-control appointments-only) x (fluoxetine 20mg vs placebo drug), n=136 randomized (33/34/35/34 per cell). Per task instructions, GET arms (exercise+fluoxetine, exercise+placebo, total n=67 randomized) were pooled vs non-GET/exercise-control arms (exercise-control+fluoxetine, exercise-control+placebo, total n=69 randomized), collapsing the drug factor. The paper itself reports this pooled exercise main-effect directly via 2-way ANOVA on change scores (F(1,132) etc.), which is exactly the GET-vs-control contrast needed - I used these pooled values rather than combining the 4 raw cells myself. Table 2 (page 4 of PDF) gives per-CELL (not pooled) mean(95% CI) for fatigue scale and mean(s.d.)/mean(95%CI) for functional work capacity at weeks 0, 0-12, 0-26, but NOT per-arm SD for fatigue at any timepoint (baseline fatigue is reported as mean with 95% CI, not SD, unlike fwc and HAD-depression which do report baseline SD). Because only pooled between-group ANOVA results (not per-arm pooled mean/SD) are directly stated in text, and the four individual factorial cells were not further pooled to synthetic mean/SD by me (would require assuming equal weighting/variance across unequal n cells, not stated in source), I report reported='between_group_only' for both outcomes with confidence=medium (numbers are exact/verbatim but the GET-vs-control arms are themselves already-pooled composites from a factorial design, and no independent per-arm SD is available to construct SMD). Trial-completer (per-protocol) sensitivity results at 26 weeks also reported in text (mean change=4.5, 95% CI 0.3-8.7, F(1,92)=4.98, P=0.028, n=96) but ITT is the primary/reported analysis and is what I used. Oxford criteria explicitly stated. Adults only (>18y). This is the trial commonly cited as 'Wearden 1998'.

physical_function.instrument: Functional work capacity (fwc) - oxygen consumption (ml O2 per kg body weight per min) in final minute of graded cycle-ergometer exercise test; NOT SF-36 or 6MWT
physical_function.scale_range: ml O2 kg-1 min-1 (no fixed upper bound; baseline means ~20-26)
physical_function.evidence_quote: There was a significant effect of exercise on functional work capacity at both weeks 12 (n=132, mean change=2.0 (95% CI 0.60-3.49); F(1,28)=7.99, P=O.OOS) and 26 (n=132, mean change=1.9 (95% CI 0.15-3.69); F(1,128)=4.74, P=0.03).

rob_notes: Randomization: computer-generated random numbers, balanced in blocks of 10, no stratification (adequate sequence generation). Allocation concealment: subject-number list with exercise-group assignment held by physiotherapist; pharmacy dispensed drug per subject number (concealment of drug allocation reasonable; concealment of exercise allocation from the randomizer/assessor less clear). Blinding: drug arm was double-blind (identical placebo capsule); exercise arm was NOT possible to blind in the usual sense - patients were told they'd receive 'one of two forms of lifestyle advice' and were blind to which, but this is a weak sham (activity-diary review as placebo control) rather than true blinding, so high risk of performance bias for the exercise contrast. Primary outcome (Chalder fatigue scale) is self-reported = high risk of detection/reporting bias given unblinded exercise allocation. Attrition: high and differential - 37% dropout in exercise vs 22% in non-exercise arms (P=0.05), handled via last-observation-carried-forward (previous assessment substituted) in ITT analysis, which is a further risk of bias (conservative but not unbiased). Outcome assessment for functional work capacity (cycle ergometer test) is more objective but still subject to effort/motivation effects post unblinded intervention.

rob_notes: Randomization: computer-generated random number sequence in sealed opaque envelopes by independent administrator (adequate allocation concealment described). Open-label design — no blinding of participants or clinicians possible given nature of intervention (exercise vs standard care); primary/secondary outcomes are entirely self-report (Fatigue Scale, SF-36, global impression of change) = high risk of performance and detection bias. Attrition: 3/25 (12%) exercise and 3/24 (12.5%) control did not complete 12-week outcome data (88% completion both groups); ITT analysis conducted substituting non-improver status/carried-forward baseline scores, results held for fatigue but note per-arm N in Table 2 reflects completers (n=22 exercise, n=21 control) not the full randomized n=25/24. Small sample (power calculated for n=27/arm but only n=25/24 achieved, so likely underpowered for physical function outcome, consistent with the null SF-36 finding). Baseline imbalance: exercise group significantly younger (36.72 vs 45.48, p=.009); age was controlled for in regression analyses. Single site, single un-blinded assessor context typical of open-label GET trials.
usable_reason: Genuine GET (12-week individualized graded exercise programme) vs non-exercise standard-medical-care control, two-arm parallel RCT with per-arm mean/SD at end-of-treatment (12 weeks) for both fatigue (14-item Fatigue Scale total score) and physical function (SF-36 PF subscale). Suitable for SMD pooling using per-arm means/SDs from Table 2.
notes: Fatigue Scale uses 0-3 item scoring (not the more common 0-11 bimodal or 0-33 Likert scoring), giving a total-score range of 0-42 for 14 items (physical fatigue subscale + mental fatigue subscale = total). When pooling as SMD this doesn't matter (scale-free), but if pooling as raw mean difference against other trials using different Chalder scoring, must convert/exclude. Between-group effect reported only as a standardized regression beta-weight (controlling for age and baseline score), not as mean-difference/CI/SMD, so no numeric MD/CI could be extracted for between_group.value/ci_low/ci_high — only beta and p are quoted in evidence_quote. Raw per-arm means/SDs (Table 2) are the more directly poolable numbers and are high-confidence. Primary study outcome per the authors was actually the dichotomous self-rated global improvement (12/22, 54.5% GET 'much/very much better' vs 5/21, 23.8% control; chi-sq=4.25, p=.04; NNT=3.2), not fatigue/physical-function per se, but fatigue and SF-36 PF are the standard outcomes needed for this meta-analysis's fatigue/physical-function pooled estimates. 6-month (42-week) follow-up data exist in Figure 1 (not extracted here per end-of-treatment instruction) showing gains maintained for physical fatigue (repeated-measures group x time interaction significant, p<.05) but not mental fatigue or physical functioning.

rob_notes: Randomization via ad hoc random-number generator; allocation performed by an author blinded to the randomization sequence (reasonable allocation concealment). No blinding of participants/providers possible (open-label CBT+GET vs usual care) -> high risk of performance bias. Outcome assessor described as independent and blinded to group assignment, but primary outcomes (SF-36, HAQ, FIS) are self-administered/self-reported questionnaires, limiting the value of assessor blinding against reporting bias. Attrition low and balanced (5/120, ~4%). CRITICAL CAVEAT: intervention arm is a combined multidisciplinary package (group CBT + GET + pharmacotherapy) vs usual treatment (exercise counselling + pharmacotherapy) -- GET's independent contribution cannot be isolated, so is_get_vs_control=false. Fatigue (FIS) was a secondary, sparsely reported outcome (no exact p or CI); primary outcome was SF-36 HRQL. The 12-month timepoint is long-term follow-up after treatment ended, not an immediate end-of-treatment assessment -- no earlier post-treatment data reported.
usable_reason: Intervention combines CBT+GET as one package vs a non-exercise usual-care control, so GET's independent effect cannot be extracted (is_get_vs_control=false). Fatigue outcome (FIS) is sparsely reported (means/SDs only, no CI/exact p) and was secondary; SF-36 physical function reflects 12-month long-term follow-up, not immediate post-treatment. Exclude from primary GET-only pooled estimate; consider only for a sensitivity analysis of combined CBT+GET packages.

get_arm_label: Maximum intervention (n=38): education about physiological basis of symptoms + individually-designed home-based graded exercise programme + 2 face-to-face sessions + 7 additional one-hour face-to-face sessions over 3 months. (Minimum intervention n=37, and Telephone intervention n=39, received the identical graded-exercise education/programme with less follow-up support; all three did not differ significantly from each other on primary outcomes, so any of the three could serve as the "GET/education-to-exercise" arm — Maximum intervention chosen here as the most intensively supported.)

harms.definition: Dropouts during treatment; reasons given (medical, psychiatric, no reason, emigrated, dissatisfied) — no explicit "serious adverse event" reporting in this paper
harms.note: 19 of 21 total dropouts were from the three intervention (education/graded-exercise) groups combined (n=114 total across 3 arms: 37+39+38), vs 2 from control (n=34). Reasons for the 19 intervention dropouts: 8 medical reasons, 7 psychiatric reasons, 4 no reason given, 1 emigrated, 1 dissatisfied with treatment. No formal serious-adverse-event or harm-specific reporting; these are all-cause treatment dropouts, not verified harms.

notes: This trial (Powell 2001, BMJ) is an educational intervention that explains the physiological basis of CFS symptoms and encourages self-managed HOME-BASED GRADED EXERCISE, delivered with varying intensity of therapist support (minimum/telephone/maximum), vs standardised medical care (which itself included an information booklet 'that encouraged graded activity' but gave no physiological explanation). It is commonly included in GET-vs-control meta-analyses (e.g. Cochrane Larun et al.) as a graded-exercise/advice trial, though it is arguably more an 'education + self-directed GET' trial than a formally supervised GET programme (unlike PACE/Fulcher-White/GETSET). There are 3 intervention arms and no significant differences were found between them ('No significant differences were found between the three intervention groups' — abstract; also confirmed in Results). Because there is no single combined-arm mean/SD reported in the paper, I selected the Maximum intervention arm (n=38) as the representative GET/education arm for the primary pool fields above, but the Minimum (n=37) or Telephone (n=39) intervention arms have nearly identical 1-year outcomes (Fatigue 1yr: 3.2, 3.5, 3.1 respectively; SF-36 PF 1yr: 25.1, 24.3, 24.9 respectively) and could equally be used, or all three could be pooled (would need pairwise combination formula since only per-arm CIs, not raw data, are available). Per-arm SDs are NOT directly reported in the source — Table 3 reports means with 95% CI only; SDs above were back-calculated from CI half-width and the ITT (randomised) n per arm: SE=(upper-lower)/(2*1.96), SD=SE*sqrt(n). This is mathematically sound but introduces some uncertainty (assumes normal approximation and that n used for CI = n randomized), hence confidence='medium' rather than 'high'. Primary outcome per the paper's own definition was the SF-36 physical-functioning subscale (dichotomized clinical-improvement criterion: score >=25 or increase >=10) plus the continuous fatigue scale score, both assessed at 12 months with ANCOVA (baseline score + depression score as covariates) — the between-group P<0.001 values reported are ANCOVA omnibus/pairwise P-values, not simple mean-difference CIs; the paper does not give an explicit MD/SMD with 95% CI for the group contrast, only per-arm means+CIs and ANCOVA P-values. No explicit serious-adverse-event reporting; dropout counts by arm are given (see harms field) but are not framed as harms specifically. Diagnostic criteria: Oxford (Sharpe et al 1991 operational criteria) explicitly stated ('148 consecutively referred patients fulfilling Oxford criteria'). Age: adults 15-55 (age_group=adult though lower bound 15 slightly overlaps adolescent; trial context and mean age ~33-34 mean it's essentially an adult sample). RoB: open-label, unblinded (patients and clinicians aware of allocation; impossible to blind an educational/exercise-advice intervention vs standard care), self-report primary outcomes (SF-36 PF and Chalder-type fatigue scale) = high risk of performance and detection bias. Randomization: 'computer generated random numbers in sealed numbered envelopes' with stratification by HADS depression cutoff — allocation concealment appears reasonable (sealed sequentially numbered envelopes) though not explicitly confirmed as opaque/tamper-evident. Attrition: 21/148 (14%) dropped out overall, asymmetric across arms (2/34 control vs 19/114 pooled intervention arms) — differential attrition is a risk-of-bias concern, though ITT-LOCF analysis was used for all randomised patients. No SF-36 raw table numbers were altered/invented; all values are transcribed directly from Table 3 of the PDF (BMJ 2001;322:387, pages 1-5 of the downloaded PDF). | PATCHED: pooled 3 intervention (education-to-encourage-graded-exercise) arms n=114 vs control n=34; SF-36 PF is Powell's 10-30 subscale, fatigue is Chalder 0-11 bimodal (source Table 3 = mean(95%CI); SDs back-converted). Intervention is patient education, NOT supervised GET -> flag + exclude-Powell sensitivity.

rob_notes: Open-label trial: patients and clinicians necessarily unblinded (education/graded-exercise intervention vs standardised medical care cannot be masked); all primary outcomes are self-reported questionnaires (SF-36 physical function, Chalder-type fatigue scale) = high risk of performance and detection bias. Randomisation via computer-generated random numbers in sealed numbered envelopes, stratified by HADS depression cutoff (>=11) — allocation concealment plausible but not explicitly detailed as tamper-evident/opaque. Differential attrition: 21/148 (14%) overall dropouts, but heavily skewed to intervention arms (19/114 in the 3 active arms vs 2/34 in control), a moderate attrition/differential-dropout risk despite ITT-LOCF analysis being used for all randomised patients. Sample size was calculated a priori (26/group, target 34/group) and achieved (148 randomised across 4 groups). No mention of blinded outcome assessors. Group comparisons for the 3 intervention arms vs each other were post hoc / not prespecified (Bonferroni-corrected).

rob_notes: Randomization: computer/random-number-table generated allocation sequence ("arranged in random order determined by random number tables"), with allocation concealed via sealed opaque envelopes prepared and opened by an independent administrator blind to psychiatrist — reasonable allocation concealment. Blinding: NOT possible for participants or treating exercise physiologists (open-label, both arms knew which active behavioral treatment they received); the assessing psychiatrist who recorded the primary outcome (self-rated clinical global impression change score) WAS blind to treatment allocation, but the primary secondary outcomes reported here (Chalder fatigue, SF-36) are self-rated by unblinded patients -- high risk of performance/detection bias for these self-report measures. Attrition: low and balanced (4/33 exercise vs 3/33 flexibility dropped out before 12-week completion; ~12% overall), intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis reported for the primary CGI outcome only, not clearly for Chalder/SF-36 (Table 3 appears to be completers-only, n=29/30). Outcome measurement: fatigue and physical function are self-report questionnaires, consistent with the open-label design's bias risk.
notes: Trial is 12 weeks of supervised graded aerobic exercise vs 12 weeks of flexibility+relaxation therapy (non-exercise, attention-matched control), n=33/33 randomized, Oxford criteria, adults, single-center UK (St Bartholomew's/Royal London). Table 3 provides per-arm mean(SD) at baseline and after 12 weeks (completers n=29 exercise, n=30 flexibility) for both Chalder fatigue and SF-36 physical function, plus a p-value column, but does NOT give an explicit between-group mean-difference estimate with 95% CI (only p-values, likely from Student's t-test per the Methods). No long-term (3-month/1-year) Chalder or SF-36 means are reported — those follow-ups only report categorical self-rated global improvement, not fatigue/function scale scores, so they cannot substitute for the 12-week endpoint. The primary outcome per the trial's own design was the self-rated Clinical Global Impression change score (not Chalder/SF-36), but per task instructions Chalder fatigue scale and SF-36 physical function are extracted here as the standardized fatigue/function outcomes for pooling. Confidence is 'high' for both because the exact per-arm n/mean/SD are directly read from the table image (cross-validated against two independent renders and against body.md's OCR text, which matched exactly).

rob_notes: Randomisation done 'by an independent investigator' - method/allocation concealment not described in detail. Open-label: 'neither subjects nor the exercise physiologist were blinded to the intervention' (explicitly stated as a limitation). Control arm (relaxation/flexibility) is an attention-placebo control, which partially addresses non-specific effects but not exercise-specific expectancy. Primary outcomes (fatigue, depression, anxiety) are self-report questionnaires -> high risk of performance and detection bias given lack of blinding. Attrition: 6/34 (18%) withdrew from exercise arm and 5/34 (15%) from relaxation arm before/during baseline testing, analysed as completers (32 and 29) - no ITT analysis reported. Small sample (n=61 analysed).
usable_reason: Genuine GET vs non-exercise (relaxation/flexibility attention-placebo) control trial with Fukuda-CDC diagnosed adults. Fatigue data usable via Chalder-scale physical/mental fatigue subscale per-arm means (n, mean) at end of 12-week treatment, though SD not reported (only 95% CI - would need back-calculation: SD = CI_halfwidth * sqrt(n) / 1.96). Physical function (SF-36/6MWT) not reported at all in this paper - only graphical physiological work-capacity data without exact numbers, so not usable for physical function pooling from this source. Recommend back-calculating SD from the 95% CI bounds given in Box 5 for fatigue if pooling.
notes: This is the Wallman/Morton/Goodman/Grove/Guilfoyle 2004 MJA trial ('Randomised controlled trial of graded exercise in chronic fatigue syndrome'), 12-week graded exercise WITH PACING vs relaxation/flexibility (attention-placebo control), Fukuda-CDC diagnosed adults (16-74 yo), N=61 analysed (32 GET, 29 control) of 68 randomised. No JATS XML was available; PDF was read directly and body.md was not used since it is known to lose tables. All numeric tables (Box 3, 4, 5, 6) were captured from the PDF render; Box 2 is a figure/graph only (values not numerically tabulated in text) so exact power-output/physical-function means+SD could not be extracted. Fatigue subscales (mental/physical) are reported as means with 95% CI (not SD) per arm at baseline and post-intervention; the group x time interaction ANOVA p-values are 0.023 (mental fatigue) and 0.074 (physical fatigue) - these are omnibus interaction p-values, not necessarily identical to a simple post-hoc between-group comparison at post-intervention alone. Depression (HADS) was significantly improved in GET vs control (interaction P=0.041; text states post-hoc P=0.027 for post-intervention group difference) - included only as context, not the primary requested outcome. No SF-36 physical function or 6MWT outcome exists in this paper.
